translation: Let me now explain the rules of chess.
Let's next explain how each piece moves.

Firstly, these are the basic rules that
govern the movement of pieces.
1. You cannot jump one piece over another.

Whether an enemy or ally piece, you cannot
make one piece jump past another.

2. You cannot move to a tile with an ally piece
in it.

Your piece may not enter a tile with an ally
piece on it. It must stop before contact.
3. You can capture the opponent's pieces.

You can move to the tile of an enemy piece by
capturing it.

Your piece cannot then continue to advance
in the same turn, and must stop on the tile.

Now that we understand the basic rules, we'll
explain how each piece moves.
1. The movement of the king.
The king is the most important piece…

…but it only moves 1 tile adjacently or
diagonally.

It cannot share a tile with an ally piece, but it
can capture the opponent's pieces.

It cannot move to tiles under attack by the
opponent's pieces.
2. The movement of the queen.
The queen is the most powerful piece in chess.

It can move freely in every direction, including
diagonals.

It cannot share a tile with an ally piece, but it
can capture the opponent's pieces.
3. The movement of the bishop.
Bishops can move freely in diagonals.
They're no different to bishops in shogi.

They cannot share a tile with an ally piece,
but they can capture the opponent's pieces.
4. The movement of the knight.
The knights move in a rather complicated way.

They move in an "L” shape, two tiles away in
any direction, and an additional tile sideways.

It's similar to a shogi knight, but it can make
the movement in any direction.

The movement is little complicated, but also
important, so try to remember it.

There is another special rule to the knight's
movement.

They are the only pieces that can jump past
other pieces.

The knights play an important role in putting
pressure on a king…
…which is hiding in its camp.
5. The movement of the rook.

Rooks can move freely forwards, backwards,
left, and right.
They are no different to rooks in shogi.

It cannot share a tile with an ally piece, but it
can capture the opponent's pieces.
6. The movement of the pawn.
Pawns can move one space forward.
They're no different to pawns in shogi.
However, pawns are a little bit complicated…
…and they have a few special rules to them.

Special rule 1. They can move up to two spaces
forward on their first move.

For each pawn, the first time it makes a move
in a game…
…it can move two spaces forward.
Special rule 2. Capturing pieces.

Normal pieces can take pieces that are within
their range of movement…

…but pawns cannot take pieces that are
directly in front of them.

In other words, if there is an enemy piece
blocking a pawn, it cannot move.

Instead, they can make a special movement
when capturing enemy pieces.

Pawns can capture pieces one square
diagonally forward from them.

The white piece on the bottom screen can
move to the highlighted tiles to capture…
…if there is an enemy piece on those tiles.

Pawns can only advance forward, not
backwards.

Remember that they can only capture enemy
pieces diagonally forward from them.
Special rule 3. En passant.

There is a special rule for pawns called "en
passant.”

Pawns can move up to two spaces forward on
their first move.

Only when a pawn has moved two spaces
forward…
…does this special rule apply.
If you have a pawn on the fifth row…

…and the opponent's pawn on the adjacent
column advances two tiles…

…you can move your pawn diagonally forward
to capture the opponent's pawn.
This is called "en passant.”

En passant is a rule that only occurs
between pawns.

Also, this rule does not apply if the
opponent's pawn makes another move…

…after they have advanced two tiles
forward.

This rule only applies directly after the
opponent makes the move.

That concludes the explanation of the pieces'
movements.
